caps.text: Of everything humans have ever made, the farthest is one small spacecraft
Voyager 1
It is so far from Earth that even light needs a whole day to reach it
It has been travelling for 49 years
And all of its computers' memory is smaller than a single photo on today's phones
Three years ago, this machine suddenly started sending meaningless signals
The same pattern, over and over
To fix it, engineers had to reason with a machine from that far away
A machine whose builders had mostly retired, and whose manuals were on paper
The next five months were the longest the Voyager team had known
But the biggest question of this story is still open
How did this human-made thing get so far...
...and when its voice falls silent forever, what will go with it?
This story begins in 1965
Until then, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, the four giant planets, were a mystery
The problem was distance
Flying straight to Neptune would take about 30 years
No machine, it seemed, could keep working that long
Then Gary Flandro, a young student working at NASA's JPL, worked out the motions of the planets
He saw that between 1976 and 1979, all four planets would line up in a special way
A chance like that comes about once every 175 years
And this line-up had an amazing advantage
When a spacecraft passes a planet, the planet's gravity pulls it and flings it onward
Just as a cricket ball speeds up off a swinging bat
Planet to planet, each time a little more speed
That cut the trip to Neptune from 30 years to just 12
Had they missed it, the next chance would come around 2150
NASA did not miss it
There was one chance, so NASA built two spacecraft
If one failed, the other would finish the job
They were named Voyager 1 and Voyager 2
But one big question remained
That far out, sunlight grows very weak
At Jupiter it is about 27 times weaker than at Earth
Solar panels can't work there
So inside each Voyager they put plutonium
Plutonium keeps giving off heat, like an ember that stays hot for years
And that heat makes electricity
That electricity keeps Voyager alive to this day
And that same electricity is slowly running out
In 1977, Voyager 2 flew first
Two weeks later, Voyager 1
Voyager 1 left later, but it was given a shorter, faster path to Jupiter
Within months, it overtook Voyager 2
But besides their science gear, both carried one more thing
A message, for someone unknown
Voyager's paths meant that after the planets, they would never come back
They would leave the solar system and wander among the stars forever
So astronomer Carl Sagan and his team decided to send a message with them
A gold-plated record, like the gramophone records of the old days
This record holds pictures of Earth
Sounds like wind, rain, and a heartbeat
Music from around the world, about 90 minutes of it
And greetings from Earth in 55 languages
One of them is in Hindi
"Greetings from the people of Earth"
The record also carries a song from India
Sung by Surshri Kesarbai Kerkar: raag Bhairavi, "Jaat Kahan Ho"
Perhaps no one will ever find it
But the record is a picture of who humans were
In space there is no air, no water, no soil to wear it down
So this picture may survive, unchanged, for a billion years
But before this message reached anyone, Voyager had a real job to do
Until 1979, scientists thought the moons of the giant planets were just cold, dead rock
In March 1979, Voyager 1 reached Jupiter
One day, NASA engineer Linda Morabito was looking at an image of Jupiter's moon Io
Her job was to check Voyager's path using the stars
Then she saw a strange cloud at the edge of Io
It was a volcano, erupting at that moment
The first active volcano ever found on any world beyond Earth
Then came Saturn
In 1980, Voyager 1 was sent close to Saturn's moon Titan
Titan has a thick blanket of air, and scientists wanted a close look
But that decision had a price
All the planets circle the Sun on nearly the same flat path, like marbles rolling on a plate
Titan's gravity did what the planets had done before
It bent Voyager 1's path up, out of the plate
Now it could never reach another planet
Voyager 2 made the rest of the journey alone
Uranus in 1986, and Neptune in 1989
To this day, Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited these two planets
The planets were done
But before Voyager 1's cameras switched off, it had one last picture to take
By 1990, Voyager 1 was about 6 billion kilometres from Earth
To save power, NASA was about to switch its cameras off for the last time
Then Carl Sagan made an odd demand
Turn the camera around, toward Earth
Many were against it
A picture of Earth from that far was of no use to science
In the end Sagan won, and Voyager looked back
